greek: καὶ ὕλην, ἀγένητον, καὶ ταύτην φασὶ συναμα- χέναι τῷ Θεῷ. Εἰ δὲ Θεὸς ἀγένητος, καὶ ὕλη ἀγένητος, οὐχ ἔτι ὁ Θεὸς ποιητὴς τῶν ὅλων ἐστὶ κατὰ τοὺς Πλατωνικούς, οὐδὲ μὴν μοναρχία Θεοῦ δείκνυται, ὅσον τὸ κατ᾽ αὑτούς.

english: But if God is uncreated and matter uncreated, God is no longer, according to the Platonists, the Creator of all things, nor, so far as their opinions hold, is the monarchy  of God established.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, as revised on New Advent)
page: page unknown (Migne PG 6, Book II, chapter as stated; column numerals not reliably read from OCR)

what_it_says: If matter is also uncreated, God is no longer the sole Creator and His monarchy is not established.
limits: 'μοναρχία' here means God's sole rule and creatorship against Platonic matter, not the later Monarchian or Unitarian sense. It is the word that Unitarians cite. The OCR line break in 'συναμα- χέναι' is a word-break: the word is συνηκμακέναι (from συνακμάζω, 'be coeval'); kept as read.

greek: Ὥσπερ οὖν ἐν τούτοις πᾶσιν δυνατώτερός ἐστιν ὁ θεὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, οὕτω καὶ τὸ ἐξ οὐχ ὄντων ποιεῖν καὶ πεποιηκέναι τὰ ὄντα καὶ ὅσα βούλεται, καθὼς βούλεται.

english: As, therefore, in all these respects God is more powerful than man, so also in this; that out of things that are not He creates and has created things that are, and whatever He pleases, as He pleases.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, as revised on New Advent)
page: page unknown (Migne PG 6, Book II, chapter as stated; column numerals not reliably read from OCR)
edition: Migne PG 6 (Paris 1857) for Greek; ANF vol. 2 (Buffalo 1885) for English
what_it_says: As God surpasses man in everything, so He creates things that are out of things that were not, as He pleases.
limits: Answer to the Platonist claim that God can only shape pre-existing matter. It is about creation out of non-being, not about the Word. Dods's 'out of things that are not' is ex ouk ontōn in Greek; 'out of nothing' is the phrase used in ch. 10, not here.

what_it_says: Some poets woke up in soul and spoke things in harmony with the prophets about the monarchy of God and judgment.

The passage shows only that Theophilus uses the word for God's sole rule, against the poets' many gods. Says nothing on the Word, Wisdom or Spirit. ref: Autol. 2.9 (Dods ch. 9 'The Prophets Inspired by the Holy Ghost')
greek: Οἱ δὲ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἄνθρωποι, πνευματοφόροι Πνεύματος ἁγίου καὶ προφῆται γενόμενοι, ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐμπνευσθέντες καὶ σοφισθέντες ἐγένοντο θεοί-δαχτοι, καὶ ὅσιοι καὶ δίκαιοι. Διὸ καὶ κατηξιώτσαν τὴν ἀντιμισθίέαν ταύτην λαθεῖν ὄργανα Θεοῦ γενόμενοι, καὶ χωρήσαντες σοφίαν τὴν παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ, δι᾽ ἧς σοφίας εἶπον καὶ τὰ περὶ τῆς χτίσεως τοῦ κόσμου καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ἁπάντων.

english: But men of God carrying in them a holy spirit  and becoming prophets, being inspired and made wise by God, became God-taught, and holy, and righteous. Wherefore they were also deemed worthy of receiving this reward, that they should become instruments of God, and contain the wisdom that is from Him, through which wisdom they uttered both what regarded the creation of the world and all other things.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2, as revised on New Advent)
page: page unknown (Migne PG 6, Book II, chapter as stated; column numerals not reliably read from OCR)
edition: Migne PG 6 (Paris 1857) for Greek; ANF vol. 2 (Buffalo 1885) for English
what_it_says: Prophets who carry the Holy Spirit become instruments of God and receive God's wisdom, through which they spoke of creation.
limits: The wisdom is given to the prophets, who are called God's 'instruments' (ὄργανα). Arian readers use 'instrument' language to make Wisdom a creature. Here the instrument is the prophets, not the Word. 'Holy Spirit' (Πνεύματος ἁγίου) is in the prophets' sense, not a person in a Trinitarian sense. Greek: 'κατηξιώτσαν', 'λαθεῖν', 'θεοί-δαχτοι' are OCR errors (read as καταξιωθῆσαν, λαβεῖν, θεοδίδακτοι).
